title: SDK surface consolidation: lazy iterators, streaming guardrails, and degradation strategy
creator: Maya Singh
description: Consolidate SDK client surfaces across Python/TS/Go to provide a single, opinionated approach for paginated iterators, resumable streaming, and deterministic retry semantics. Produce concrete acceptance criteria, client API sketches, and a compatibility/deprecation plan so teams can adopt with minimal friction.
background: Multiple SDKs currently expose varying iterator patterns (async generators, callbacks, custom cursor objects) and inconsistent retry behaviour. This causes customer confusion, increases SDK maintenance burden, and complicates server-side rollout/compatibility. Goal: one converged pattern per language family that supports resumable pagination and streaming, clear retry boundaries, and graceful degradation to lower-capacity model variants.
scope: Define API and behavioral contracts for: (1) paginated fetch primitives (lazy iterators and cursor tokens), (2) streaming responses with explicit resume/checkpoint semantics and backpressure handling, (3) client-side retry classification and idempotency guarantees, and (4) compatibility matrix and deprecation plan for existing methods. Produce PRD, acceptance tests, and migration guide for SDK teams.
out_of_scope: Rewriting existing SDK implementations end-to-end (engineering will implement in follow-up tickets), platform-side routing/fallback implementation details, and changes to server-side cursor/token formats beyond stable compatibility constraints.
requirements: Single paginated iterator pattern per language that supports lazy retrieval and resume via opaque cursor tokens
Streaming API must expose a resumable checkpoint and explicit client-visible backpressure controls (prefetch limits or pull signals)
Retry contract: non-idempotent operations must not be retried by default; idempotent read and list operations must support configurable retry policies with exponential backoff and jitter
SDKs must offer a compatibility shim layer to map legacy iterator forms to the new surface for at least two minor releases
Clear semantic versioning and deprecation notice process documented in the migration guide
Automated acceptance tests that validate resume semantics across short disruptions and common error classes
Client libraries must include example migration snippets for Python, TypeScript, and Go
api_surface_changes: Python: introduce 'Client.paginated_iter' returning an async iterator that yields items and exposes 'cursor' on the iterator to snapshot progress
TypeScript: expose 'client.listStream()' returning an AsyncIterable with a 'checkpoint()' method that returns opaque token string
Go: provide 'ListIterator' with Next() and Cursor() methods, and a constructor that accepts an optional startCursor string
All languages: expose 'resume_from(cursor)' or equivalent factory/constructor parameter to restart a stream/list from a server-validated cursor
pagination_contract: Iterators must be lazy (no prefetch of full page set) and must not surface implementation internals (no raw page objects). Opaque cursors are stable across minor releases; servers may reject invalid cursors with a well-documented error class 'InvalidCursorError' (retryable=false). Clients must document expected staleness and provide best-effort resume semantics under transient failures.
streaming_contract: Streaming responses should be cancellable by the client and resumable via checkpoint tokens emitted periodically. Streams must surface connection health and allow the application to apply backpressure (through pull or credit-based APIs). When resuming, the server will guarantee at-most-once replay from the last emitted checkpoint; clients accepting possible duplication must handle idempotency at application layer or opt-in to server deduplication where available.
retry_contract: Define three error classes: transient (retryable), throttling (retryable with backoff and rate limit awareness), and permanent (do not retry). Default retry policy: 3 attempts with exponential backoff (base=200ms, factor=2, max=3s) and randomized jitter. SDKs must allow override of retries per-call and expose hooks for custom logic. Non-idempotent write/modify endpoints default to retries disabled; explicit idempotency tokens may enable safe retries.
compatibility_matrix: Minimum supported runtime versions: Python 3.10+, Node 18+, Go 1.20+. Backwards compatibility: SDKs will support legacy iterator methods via a compatibility shim for two minor releases; new major release will remove old methods with migration guide published 8 weeks prior. Compatibility scenarios documented for server-induced cursor invalidation and incremental server rollout (fallback to list-by-page API when stream resume is not yet supported).
acceptance_criteria: SDK API sketches approved by Eng/Design/PM
Automated tests demonstrate successful resume of paginated iterator after simulated connection interruption (Python/TS/Go)
Retry policy unit tests validate no default retries for non-idempotent calls and correct backoff behavior for transient errors
Compatibility shim passes integration smoke tests against current production endpoints
Migration guide with examples for main use-cases (list, stream, long poll) published in docs and referenced from SDK READMEs
Performance regression <5% p95 latency for list/stream common-case in each SDK after shims are added (benchmarks attached)
rollout_plan: Phase 1: PRD and API sketches (this ticket). Phase 2: prototype shim in Python and TS (ENG follow-ups). Phase 3: integration tests and docs. Phase 4: gradual rollout with opt-in in SDK nightly builds, collect telemetries (error rates, resume success rate), and flip default after 4 weeks if metrics stable. Phase 5: deprecate legacy methods with staged notices.
test_plan: Create acceptance test harness that can simulate: short TCP drop, auth token refresh, server-side cursor rotation. For each language: unit tests for iterator semantics, integration tests against staging server, e2e test that validates checkpoint tokens persist and allow resume. Add perf benchmarks to validate latency impact.
